## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kaṇṇakatthala Sutta* (MN 90) is set at Ujuññā in Kaṇṇakatthala, where King Pasenadi of Kosala visits the Buddha [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Peoples 2013]. Pasenadi questions the Buddha on several distinct subjects, including claims of omniscience, the spiritual equality of caste distinctions, and the existence and nature of the gods [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Within early canonical literature, the sutta and its Chinese counterpart are distinctive for featuring an active spoken intervention by Viḍūḍabha (Virūḍhaka) rather than portraying him as a silent figure [Bareau, Le Bouddha et les rois]; it also mentions two sisters, Somā and Sakulā [Galasek 2016].
A primary focus of the sutta is defining the Buddhist position on omniscience (*sabbaññutā*). Clarifying a widespread misrepresentation, the Buddha explains that he does not deny that a recluse or brahmin can have complete vision, but explicitly rejects the notion that anyone can know all and see all simultaneously (*sakideva sabbaṁ ñassati sabbaṁ dakkhīti*) [Appleton, Narrating Karma and Rebirth; Endo 1997; Le 2018]. The Pali commentary glosses this phrase as knowing or seeing everything across the past, future, and present in a single mental adverting (*ekāvajjanena*), single thought (*ekacittena*), and single impulse (*ekajavanena*) [Endo 1997; Le 2018]. In contrast to continuous simultaneous knowledge, the Buddha claims the threefold knowledge (*tevijjā*) [Endo 1997; Pande 1974; Le 2018]. Regarding social hierarchy, the Buddha instructs the king that individuals from all four social classes possess the capacity to strive towards spiritual perfection without inherent disparity [Peoples 2013].
Curated parallels include MĀ 212 in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (T 26, p. 793b) and D 1 in the Tibetan Kangyur [SuttaCentral; Bareau, Le Bouddha et les rois]. DharmaNexus confirms these alignments via matches with the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (ZH_T01_0026_059) and the Tibetan *Vinayavastu* (BO_K01_D0001-2), alongside cross-language matches in the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu* and *Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra* [DharmaNexus]. In the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records 1,950 reuse matches across 125 texts, including substantial shared passages with the *Kosala Saṁyutta* (SN 3), the *Pañcakanipāta* (AN 5), and the *Bodhirājakumāra Sutta* (MN 85, sharing an extensive section on spiritual striving at §10.6–10.17) [DharmaNexus].
